Executive summary
Introduction

A key purpose of standardization is to enable multivendor interoperability, i.e., to allow implementations from different vendors to work together. In particular, standardization of management interfaces should simplify management of mobile networks (e.g. 3GPP TS 32.101 [i.12]). In 3GPP SA5, the concept of management services is used as described in TS 28.533 [i.4].

To support interoperability, it is fundamental that (Management) Service Producer and (Management) Service Consumer(s) agree on use cases and requirements. Then, based on use cases and requirements, a model of the information to be managed must be agreed between producer and consumers and according to those, a specific solution set, in terms ofprotocol and data model, must be also defined and agreed.

3GPP uses a phased approach defined in 21.900. In 3GPP SA5, in general, Stage 1 specifications define requirements and use cases. Stage 2 specification define the managed entities in terms of a common information model that consumers and producers shallagree on and exchange to realize the use cases defined in stage 1. Stage 3 specification defines specific solution sets that implement the models defined at stage 2.

The service-based management architecture in TS 28.533 [i.4] defines a management service to be composed of management operations and/or notifications (referred to asManagement Service Component Type A), data to be

managed (referred to asManagement Service Component Type B) and fault and performance information (referred to as Management Service Component Type C). The latter component is optional in the definition of a management service. The O-RAN O1 specification [i.1] largely consists ofreferences to Stage 2 and Stage 3 instantiations ofthese three component types.

In this report, we visit each of these component types and examine whether emerging cloud-native management design patterns might motivate the creation of new Stage 1 requirements and use cases, new Stage 2 operations and information models, and new Stage 3 protocols and transport mechanisms. We begin in clause 4 with Management Component Type B, as information and data models are foundational to our study. Then clause 5 examines Management Component Type A, the set of operations and notifications defined to work on the data. clause 6 examines the controlaspects of Management Component Type C and clause 7 examines transport of those fault, performance, and trace information from a cloud-native perspective.
1 Scope

The objective of this Technical Report is to study the data formats, management operations, and telemetry transport mechanisms for OAM from a cloud-native perspective. Where applicable, the presentdocument proposes recommendations or potential solutions for cloud-native OAM.

4 Analysis of Data Format
4.1 Background
4.1.1 MnS Component Type B

A Management Service Component Type B is defined in clause 4.2.3.1 of 3GPP TS 28.533 [i.4] as referring to management information represented by information models representing the managed entities. The definition goeson to state that the terminology "MnS component type B" is interchangeable with the term "Network Resource Model (NRM)". Two examples ofNRMs are given, one being the generic NRM 3GPP TS 28.622 [i.6] and one being the 5G NRM 3GPP TS 28.541 [i.5].

3GPP TS 32.156 [i.8] defines a model repertoire for building abstract information models of network resources. It outlines a subset of the Unified Modeling Language (UML) to be used in model development. It defines the stereotype Information Object Class (IOC) as a key building block for information models. To define a new IOC, a modeler gives it a class name and an associated table of attributes, each of which can take on a range of usually primitive or simple compound values according to its data type. The repertoire also defines the <<names>> stereotype association which allows one class to name-contain other classes. The name-containment relationship can be single (represented with [ParentIOC] 1 <<names>> 0..1 [Child IOC] in the UML diagram) or multiple (represented with [ParentIOC] 1 <<names>> * [ChildIOC] in the UML diagram). Typically, when a 3GPP document defines a collection of IOCs, the name-containment relationships are specified with a collection of diagrams in a separate clause of the document from the per-IOC clauses that define the attributes ofeach new class.

References to specific object instances are implemented with the concept of a Distinguished Name (DN) from the X.500 family of specifications [i.2]. References to specific object instances are important to express a non-containment association from one object instance to another, as well as to indicate which object is the subjectof a management operation as described in clause 5. A DN as used by the name convention for managed objects 3GPP TS 32.300 [i.10] is a sequence of Attribute Type, Attribute Value pairs; the Attribute Type is a string containing the class name of the ChildIOC, and the AttributeValue is a string containing the value of the designated "naming attribute" of the ChildIOC. This "naming attribute" is usually called "id".
4.1.2 Current Solution Set Methodology for Component Type B

To enable actual management of a network resource, the abstract information model must be converted into a Stage 3 specification that enables interoperable implementations ofmanagement operations on the modeled data. Several so called Solution Sets have been defined by 3GPP, including based on CORBA, NETCONF/YANG, and OpenAPI [i.aaa, i.ee]. Below we outline the conventions in the 3GPP managementservices template [i.eee] for OpenAPI/JSON schema and NETCONF/YANG even if current O1 specification [i.1] mandates the use of the YANG Stage 3 solution set rather than the OpenAPI/YAML Stage 3 solution set.

Here, a DemoFunction-Single Managed Object Class (MOC) of the solution set is defined corresponding to the DemoFunction Information Object Class (IOC) from the information model. A Managed Object Instance (MOI) of a DemoFunction-Single will be a JSON object that conforms to the Top MOC (which defines the id naming attribute) and will also contain an attributes property object. The attributes object conforms to the base class ManagedFunction-Attr and also contains a set of properties defined for the DemoFunction including demoId, demoFlag, and exampleConf.

In addition to the attributes object, a DemoFunction-Single conforms to the the ManagedFunction-nc0 MOC and has additional properties corresponding to the name-containment relations defined in the UML diagram for the DemoFunction IOC, including multiple ChildClass and a single AnotherChildClass.
4.1.2.2 NETCONF/YANG Data Models
A fragment of the NETCONF/YANG from the 5G NRM [i.5] is shown below:

module demofunction { …
grouping DemoFunctionGrp {
 description "Represents the DemoFunction IOC.";
 reference "Example";
 uses mf3gpp:ManagedFunctionGrp;
 leaf demoId {
  type int64 { range "0..68719476735"; }
  mandatory true;
  description "Uniquely identifies the Demo Object at least within a gNB.";
  reference "Example";
 }
 leaf demoFlag {
  type boolean;
  mandatory true;
  description "Turns on something";
  reference "Example";
 }
 list exampleConf {
  key confId;
  config false;
  min-elements 1;
  max-elements 1;
  description "Used to configure something";
  uses ExampleConfGrp;
 }
}
augment "/me3gpp:ManagedElement" {
 list DemoFunction {
  key id;
  description "Represents the logical Demo function of gNB or en-gNB.";
  reference "Example";
  uses top3gpp:Top_Grp;

Here, the attributes from the DemoFunction IOC are defined inside a YANG grouping DemoFunctionGrp, which in turn is placed inside a YANG container named attributes within each element of a list of DemoFunctions. The module augments the base ManagedElement module to contain such a list, which means that any NETCONF server claiming to implement the demofunction may contain a list of DemoFunctions inside its ManagedElement.

Note that with this approach, the definition of an MOC does not declare its child name-containment relationships, but rather expresses its parent's name containment relations of itself. This is in contrast to the OpenAPI / JSON Schema approach where the child name-containment relations are given in the parentMOC.
4.1.3 Extensibility

O1 specifications refer to 3GPP modelsfor the modelling of the logical RAN entities. 3GPP NRM models are defined in 3GPP TS 28.621[i.16] and 28.622[i.6], related YANG solution set is defined in TS 28.623 while YANG mapping rules and vendor extension mechanisms are defined in TS 32.160 [i.9].
Each 3GPP solution set has defined its own set of mapping rules and vendor extension mechanisms to provide a consistent set of models.
Extensibility mechanisms can be used to add non-standardized contents through vendor specific entities in addition to the standardized ones.

In general, the 3GPP Vendor specific extensibility mechanisms can be used by a vendor or by an SDO. In the contextof O-RAN Alliance, theO-RAN Alliance community can use vendor specific extensibility mechanisms and define a new standardized data model as O-RAN YANG modules. An O1 producer or consumer to be O1 compliantwill have to support new standardized data models.
Vendor extensions to a 3GPP YANG module can be done to:
1) Marking in a 3GPP YANG modules as "not supported" any optional element according to supportQualifier and/or any deviations that maintain backward compatibility as defined in RFC 7950
Vendor extensions to a 3GPP YANG module shall be done in a separate YANG module using augmentation mechanism:

• 1) Add vendor specific attributes to a 3GPP specified IOC
  • 2) Add a new vendor specific IOC
In case 2 and 3, the vendor extensions are name contained in an existing 3GPP IOC and the new IOC shall follow 3GPP TS 32.160 [i.9] methodology.
3GPP TS 32.160 [i.9] provides examples ofcase 2) and 3) as follows:
Example 1 – Add a vendor specific attribute to a 3GPP specified IOC:

augment /me3gpp:ManagedElement/attributes {
leaf isCabinetClosed {
 type boolean ;
 description "Indicates whether the doors ofthe HW cabinet is closed." ;
}
}
Example 2 – Add a vendor specific IOC:

//vendor class
grouping VendorClassGrp {
uses top3gpp:Top_Grp; container attributes { uses VendorClassGrp ;
}
} }

4.2 Issues and Recommendations
//YANG lists representing contained classes
4.2.1 Non-3GPP Information and Data Models

The information modeling methodology and solution sets described in clause 4.1 lead to a very particular and stylized use of YANG and OpenAPI constructs when specifying data models. This arises because of the separation of the attributes of an IOC from the name-contained relationships to other IOCs, and the enforcement of this separation with conventions such as declaring an "attributes" container for each MOC and expressing name-containment with property names (in the case of OpenAPI/YAML) or the "augments" construct (in the case of YANG). (The current O1 specification mandates the use of the YANG Stage 3 solution set rather than the OpenAPI/YAML Stage 3 solution set and so we restrict our discussion to the YANG Stage 3 solution set in what follows).

Non-3GPP SDOs do not necessarily follow the 3GPP methodology of separately modeling the information to be managed at an abstract level and then mapping these models into solution sets. Indeed, many extant YANG specifications from the IETF community are written and edited directly in YANG and make use of the full power of that notation to define data models that, for instance, do not place attributes into a container named "attributes" and which don't enforce name-containment conventions. The O-RAN Alliance WG4 has developed such a model for the OpenFH M-plane. Finally, vendor-specific YANG models also exist for which no prior information model was developed.

It is not immediately obvious that non-3GPP data models need to be managed via the O1 interface. Perhaps, these models can always be relegated to being managed over other interfaces. For example, the OpenFH M-plane is depicted

as its own interface, separate from O1, and transport elements that are likely to make use of IETF-defined models could be managed solely through a specific interface (not O1) dedicated to that purpose. However, non-3GPP data models may in fact touch the O1 interface in several ways:

• 1. For the Hierarchical O-RU management model, the O-DU exposes the O-RUs to the SMO via its own O1 interface [i.13]. This has led O-RAN WG5 to propose the embedding of the WG4 OpenFH M-plane data model on a schema mount-point within the 3GPP-compliant O-DU data model [i.14]. Operations that modify the data inside the schema mount cannot refer to MOIs by distinguished name because the OpenFH M-plane is not structured as name-contained MOIs.
  • 2. Although the transport elements themselves may be managed with a separate interface, the O-RAN Network Functions may need to borrow some of the data models to allow for configuration of the connection points where they touch the transport network. Borrowing these models literally from other domains like the IETF instead of defining new 3GPP-compliant ones would lead to simplified operational workflows. Again, these models may not be structured as name-contained MOIs.
  • 3. Any other data models, such as vendor-specific YANGs, that were not developed according to the methodology in 32.156 may also have theirown inherent structure which doesnot follow the name-contained MOI conventions. These YANG models may be embedded in a 3GPP or ORAN-compliant data model, or they may appear as a separate tree rooted at the top level of the management service.

Currently, the O-RAN OAM Architecture [i.13] and O1 interface specification [i.1] define the O1 interface for management of O-RAN Network Functions as a collection of SBMA-compliant Management Services. The existing Stage 2 operations and Stage 3 solution sets defined in 3GPP 28.532 [i.3] assume that the Management Component Type B (NRM) was developed according to the 3GPP methodology outlined in clause 4.1, and therefore cannot be used directly to manage data without distinct attributes and name-contained MOIs. One fundamental reason is that, as outlined in 3GPP TS 32.300 [i.10] clause 4.1, the names ofManaged Objects, in the form of Distinguished Names, are passed across various Integration Reference Points (IRPs) and are fundamental to the definition of the operations and cross-references between objects. These limitations will be further outlined in clause 5 of the presentdocument.
4.2.1.1 Issue Summary

Considering data models in general and theoretically, and without declaring any normative requirements in this clause, data to be managed could take any of the following forms, in decreasing order of strictness:

• 1. Structured data (e.g., JSON or XML data) that conform to a standardized 3GPP Information Model and a YANG data model developed in conformance to the conventions outlined in 3GPP 32.160;
  • 2. Structured data (e.g., JSON or XML data) that conform to a standardized YANG data model that was developed outside of 3GPP conventions, such as in the IETF or O-RAN WG4;
  • 3. Structured data (e.g., JSON or XML data) that conform to a non-standardized YANG data model that was developed outside of 3GPP conventions, such as a vendor-specific model;
  • 4. Structured data (e.g., JSON or XML data) that do not have a YANG data model;

Management of even more loosely structured or unstructured data is also a theoretical possibility but is out of scope for now. Because each of the listed data model sets is a subset of the one that comes after, any management scheme that handles one of the above sets ofdata models can also handle any of the ones listed before it.
4.2.1.2 Recommendations
We conclude that O-RAN management systems and interfaces should be capable of managing any data of types 1 – 2 from clause 4.2.1.1.
5 Analysis of Management Operations
5.1 Background
5.1.1 MnS Component Type A

Management Service Component Type A is defined in clause 4.2.2 of the 3GPP managementand orchestration architecture framework 3GPP TS 28.533 [i.4] as a group of management operations and/or notifications that is agnostic with regard to the entities managed. By "agnostic" it is meant that the operations and/or notifications can be defined

independently of any particular NRM (component type B) because the managed object instances and their data are carried in the payload of the operations ("signature of the operations", in the words of the architecture framework), but the operations themselves can be applied to many different NRMs.

The 3GPP generic management service specification 3GPP TS 28.532 [i.3], for example, defines a generic provisioning management service. In the stage 2 level of specification in clause 11.1 of 28.532, the operations, notifications, and their parameters are described without regard to how they would be encoded in a stage 3 solution set. Later in clause 12.1, a RESTful HTTP-based solution set is defined that describes how to encode these parameters into an HTTP protocol. In clause 12.1.3, it is specified how these operations and parameters would be encoded in a YANG/Netconf-based solution set.

5.2 Common Issues and Recommendations
5.2.1 Declarative vs. Imperative Pattern
5.2.1.1 Introduction

Declarative and Imperative patterns are different paradigms that describe whether or not to describe the "how". In operations applying an imperative pattern, the "how" is described explicitly by step-by-step instructions; in operations applying a declarative pattern, the desired state is managed, without explicitly describing about "how" to achieve it.

In the context of this specification, the declarative pattern provides the abstraction to get the element to the desired state. For example, declarative pattern for configuration management involves specifying the desired configuration state rather than explicitly detailing the steps needed to achieve that state.
5.2.1.2 Issue Summary

5.3.1.1 Overview

A logically centralized entity or repository hosting the desired configurations for O-RAN NFs intended to be further synchronized to a target NF residing in an O-Cloud environment based on a declarative description. It is referred as logically centralized because the realization of the repository for configuration can be multiple and distributed. Configuration repository is referred as a source of truth in the context of configuration data of NFs and configuration data related to O-Cloud.

Such configuration repository enables access to the configuration data to consumer of configuration data. In the context of provisioning of configuration data, the producer of provisioning management services uses the configuration repository to store the configuration data.

5.3.2.1 Overview
In the O-RAN system, MOIs are representing the management aspects of an O-RAN NF instance. Changes in the MOIs of O-RAN NFs may occur for reasons including, but not limited to, the following:

• 1)Software Updates and Upgrades: O-RAN NFs and rAPPs/xAPPs update and upgrade may result in MOIs value and status change.
  • 2)RAN Scaling: New O-RAN NF deployment, scaling, migration or other LCM operations in response to the capacity optimization requirement, the O-RAN NF LCM may trigger configuration changes reflected in the O-RAN NF MOI, e,g., vnfParametersList modifications as defined in [i.6].
  • 3)Fault Recovery: In the event of a NF fault, configuration changes may be needed to isolate problematic NFs, or enable fault recovery.
  • 4)Security Updates: The encryption settings as one kind of configuration data will be updated with the development of new integrity and encyption algorithms.5)Integration of New Technologies/Features: The integration of new technologies, such as the introduction of new
  • spectrum bands, Carrier Aggregation (CA), sidelink, network slice, etc., usually requires configuration changes to the corresponding features.
  • 6)Automated RAN Management: With the introduction of AI/ML in RAN, networks are progressively becoming automated. The O1 interface specification defines usage of the following solution set:
- YANG/Netconf-based solution set

Netconf (Network Configuration) protocol is a standard interface for installing, deleting and modifying the configuration data on network devices. A consumer of provisioning management service that makes use of the solution set listed above (YANG/Netconf-based solution set), requires a change in the transport mechanism for supporting the cloud friendly RESTful HTTP-based protocol for configuration management operations, to make use of commands or APIs for management of configuration data while interworking with the provisioning MnF.

6 Analysis of Operations for Telemetry Control
6.1 Background
6.1.1 MnS Component Type C

MnS component type C, as defined in 3GPP TS 28.533, represents the performance and fault information of managed entities. It provides essential data for monitoring and maintaining the operational health of network elements, facilitating effective performance management and fault detection. MnS component type C exposes management data to RAN NF OAM SMOS.Performance information, fault information are network management data collected from the network (including e.g. service, slicing and/or network functions related data). RAN analytics SMOs can consume RAN NF OAM SMOs to utilize the network management data and make the corresponding analytics based on the collected information. The performance information provided by RAN NF MnS producer can be used to optimize network performance, and the fault information provided by RAN NF MnS producer can be used to predict and prevent failures of the network.

Mobile networks have the capability to support a wide variety of services and requirements. This, along with increasing flexibility of the network may present management and operational challenges and complexities. The management system can therefore benefit from management data analytics services for improving networks performance and efficiency to accommodate and support the diversity of services and requirements.
MnS component type C consists ofbelow primary elements:

• Performance Data is defined in[i.28], 3GPP TS 28.552 and TS 28.554.
  • Alarm Information is described in 3GPP TS 28.532 and TS 28.111.
NOTE: The alarm information also includes alarms defined in O-RAN WG10 WI O-RAN-WG10.O1.Alarms, which will be referenced here once the O-RAN-WG10.O1.Alarms specifications are published.

Traces information as defined in TS 32.421 and TS 32.423.Trace information is diverse, and it mainly supports troubleshooting and validation testing. The Trace records should contain Information Elements or signaling messages from control signaling and/or the characteristics of the user data.

Together with MnS component type A and MnS component type B, MnS component type C forms a comprehensive management service that supports the configuration, monitoring, and optimization of network resources.

In the O-RAN architecture, MnS component type C can be accessed through the O1 interface. The SMO utilizes the O1 interface to collect and process MnS component type C information, enabling the monitoring and management of the performance and fault status ofO-RAN NFs. MnS component type C can also be provided to the Non-Real-Time RIC through the RAN NF OAM SMOS producer in the SMO, enabling intelligent network performance optimization, fault detection, and recovery.
6.1.2 Performance Metrics

3GPP TS 32.401 defines the concept of Performance Management activity as one to collect data, which can be used to verify the physical, virtual, and logical configuration of the network and to locate potential problems as early as possible. The type of data to be collected is defined by the equivalent measurements (e.g., as specified in 3GPP TS 32.

425 for E-UTRAN related performance measurements, and 3GPP TS 28.552 for NR related performance measurements). O-RAN O1 InterfaceSpecification refers to 3GPP 28.622 for the performance management job operation, based on the PerfMetricJob IOC, where a MnS consumer lists the performance measurements to be produced (performance metrics are identified by name). All object instances below and including the instance name-containing the PerfMetricJob are scoped for performance metric production.

In measurement data reporting, according to 3GPP 32.404, a performance measurement includes the measurement object class, describing the measured object class level where the measurement has been collected (e.g. NRCellCU, NRCellRelation).
Performance measurements, which are a permanent source of information, provide values aggregated on an observation period.
6.1.3 Events and Alarms

Event is defined as network occurrences which have significance for the management of an NE (Network Element) in clause 3.1 Terms of 3GPP TS 28.111 [i.21], for example a configuration change, a threshold crossing, a transition to an error state or a transition to a failure state. Events do not have state.
3GPP TS 28.111 [i.21] defines in clause 3.1 Terms, an alarm as a representation of an error or failure that requires attention or reaction by an operator or some machine. Alarms have state.
6.1.4 Traces

Introduction of 3GPP TS 32.421 [i.19] cites that Subscriber and equipment trace provide very detailed information at call level on one or more specific mobile(s). Such data is an additional source of information to Performance Measurements and allows going further in monitoring and optimization operations.Subscriber and Equipment (UE) Trace give instantaneous values for a specific event (e.g. call, location update, etc.). Subscriber tracing includes tracing of IMSI or Public User Identity, and equipment (UE) tracing includes tracing of IMEI or IMEISV. Trace is the easy way to go deeper into investigation and network optimization.
The use cases for Trace can be divided into two basic categories:

• Troubleshooting use cases cover situations where the operator is solving an existing problem in the operator network.
  • Validation testing use cases cover situations where the operator is not solving a known problem but merely analyzing, fine-tuning or optimizing the network.
Subscriber and UE Trace are commonly used for the purposes (to list a few) such as:

• Checking radio coverage in certain areas, testing radio coverage on a particular geographical area following network extension for instance (e.g. new site installation) by collecting RLF reports,
  • Fine-tuning and optimization of algorithms/procedures; Trace data are used to get feedback on the network quality and capacity after optimization operations like parameter fine-tuning, for instance, by using measurement data (Measurement Report).
  • Periodic sampling of network performance.

7.2 Performance Metric Transport
7.2.1 Overview
The transport of performance metric specified in O1 specifications is file-based (bulk) and/or streaming (real time).

For file-based (bulk) performance data reporting, PM data pull-based file reporting method and/or the PM data push based file reporting method is supported. Asynchronous notifyFileReady notification event is supported when PM File(s) is ready for retrieval or asynchronous notifyFilePreparationError notification event is supported when there is any error while preparing the file(s), which is optional for push-based file reporting. When transferring files, a secure connection is established from or to the File Management MnS Producer (SFTP, FTPeS or HTTPs) as defined in clause 7.1.3 of 3GPP TS 28.537 [i.29].
Performance data file content and file naming is as specified in clause 11.3.2.1 of 3GPP TS 28.532 [i.3].
Performance data file XML Format is as specified in clause 12.3.2 of 3GPP TS 28.532 [i.3] and/or in clause 4.1 of 3GPP TS 32.432 [i.30].

For performance data streaming, A secure WebSocket connection is established between the Performance Assurance MnS Producer and the Performance Assurance MnS Consumer. The description of performance data streaming is in clause 7.1.2 Transport of Performance Metrics in Current SBMA Solution Sets ofthe presentdocument.
7.2.2 Issue summary

Figure 7.2.2-1 provides an example of PM data streaming based on WebSocket architecture. During failover scenario, MnS producer need to reestablish WebSocket connection to MnS consumer as indicated by red arrow in Figure 7.2.2-1.
Figure 7.2.2-1 An Example of PM data streaming based on WebSocket
WebSocket is point-to-point persistent connection. To maintain it, streaming data reporting MnS producer and consumer need keep alive messages, that costs extra resource.

WebSocket is stateful connection in nature. Streaming data reporting MnS producer and consumer need to maintain state or consider stateless solution in cloud-native deployments, which introduces architectural and operational complexities.

WebSocket doesn't support auto-reconnect by default. WebSocket reconnection time mainly depends on failure detection time and reconnection strategy according to configuration. WebSocket reconnection interrupt time may impact PM data streaming transmission.
WebSocket doesn't support message queueing. To ensure delivery guarantees, Streaming data reporting MnS producer and consumer need additional processing.
7.2.3 Potential solution

Compared with WebSocket, Kafka is a message bus (not point-to-point) and stateless, so MnS producer and consumer don't need to maintain peer state. Other issues described in clause 7.2.2 are also handled by Kafka which is described in clause 7.3.3.

  • 3. Kafka protocol includes group id which guarantees multiple consumers in one group have load balancing and fail-over capability. In addition, Kafka heart-beat interval is short (second level), so failure detection is soon.
  • 4. Kafka is not only a protocol, but also a product which handles all aspects ofload balance, fault-tolerance and data integrity. It enables application layer to push these features to transport layer.

7.4 Trace Transport
7.4.1 Overview

The transport of trace specified in O1 specifications is file-based (bulk) and/or streaming (real time).File-based trace collects trace records in files that are available to the consumer with a time delay. The producer optionally sends the file directly to the consumer or sends the location of the file to the consumer.

Procedures for naming the trace data file are described in 3GPP TS 32.423[i.27] clause B. File Naming Convention is described in 3GPP TS 32.423[i.27] clause B.1. Trace files are produced in XML format. The XML format is described in 3GPP TS 32.423[i.27] clause A2.2. Example XML files are provided in 3GPP TS 32.423[i.27] Annex D.
In the case of streaming trace, the data is sent in bursts across a WebSocket connection to the consumer, maintaining the relevance of the data while minimizing transport overhead.

Definitions oftrace record content for all trace types, XML trace file format, and streaming trace GPB record definition are found in 3GPP TS 32.423[i.27]. definitions for streaming data reporting are specified in 3GPP TS 28.532[i.3].

For trace data streaming, A secure WebSocket connection is established between the Trace MnS Producer and the Trace MnS Consumer. The description of trace data streaming is in clause 7.1.3 Transport of Traces in Current SBMA Solution Sets of the presentdocument.
